title: Betrayal at Peor and a Priest's Spear
overview: On the edge of the promised land, many Israelites join the worship of a local god, and a deadly plague, an order to execute the guilty leaders, and one priest's violent act follow.

parts.label: Israel joins Baal of Peor (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Camped at Shittim, just across the Jordan from the land they were about to enter, Israelite men slept with Moabite women and joined their sacrificial feasts. Baal means "lord" and Peor was a mountain there, so eating the meal and bowing down bound them to that local god instead of the LORD who had led them out of Egypt.

parts.label: Orders to execute leaders (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: The LORD orders the leaders responsible to be killed and their bodies displayed in daylight, a public disgrace meant to turn away his anger. Moses passes the order to the judges, telling each to kill the men in his group who had joined this worship, though the chapter does not say how it was carried out.

parts.label: Phinehas kills a couple (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: While people wept at the tent of meeting, Israel's portable shrine, an Israelite man openly brought in a Midianite woman, and Phinehas, the high priest's son, followed them into a tent and speared them both. The word for this tent is unusual and its exact meaning is unclear; a plague then stopped, though 24,000 had died.

parts.label: A lasting priesthood promised (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: God says Phinehas shared his own fierce devotion and gives him a "covenant of peace," promising that his family line would hold the priesthood. The text calls the killing an act that "made atonement," meaning it repaired the broken relationship, and many readers find this approval of violence hard to sit with.

parts.label: The couple named (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Zimri was a family leader in the tribe of Simeon, and Kozbi was the daughter of a Midianite chief. Naming them shows this involved people of rank, which also meant Phinehas risked revenge from powerful families.

parts.label: Hostility toward Midian (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: God tells Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies, saying they deliberately lured Israel into this worship. A later chapter, Numbers 31, links the plan to the prophet Balaam and describes a brutal war against Midian.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read Phinehas's violent zeal: some see it as a lawful act of judgment God approved in that specific setting, while others see it as a troubling episode tied to its ancient context that must be read in light of Jesus' teaching on violence.
think: When does passionate devotion to something a person holds sacred become dangerous, and who should get to decide where that line is?
